column1: # Curated help for the keys worth explaining. Hand-written, and deliberately NOT
# produced by gen-schema.py: that file is regenerated from a device and would
# overwrite anything written here. Merged with it by name, in the browser.
# The rows for keys in settings.tsv describe what the odi-oss image does with
# them. The rest describe the stock firmware -- /etc/runomci.sh for how a key
# reaches omci_app, and measurement for the rest -- and are shown only in the
# read-only stock-keys view. Where a claim is not grounded it says so rather
# depends  KEY=VALUE, joined by &. When unmet the UI says the key is ignored,
#          because that is what the firmware does with it.

column3: help
column4: options

column3: Becomes `omci_app -t`. Anything outside the listed values falls back to bridge. Switching between HGU and SFU also needs a CS factory reset — this key alone leaves a stale WAN entry behind and the ONU keeps running as a router.
column4: 0=0 — SFU / bridge|1=1 — HGU / router|2=2 — hybrid

column3: Bitmask, DECIMAL -- `flash set` accepts nothing else. Passed as `omci_app -cr`. Each bit loads one plugin from lib/features; the field below decodes it. Bit 0x4 is `ignore_conn_uniNode_check`, which suppresses the ME 171 uniNode association check; the stock firmware ships with 4. On the 2024 firmware that same bit also skips populating the resolved association, which stops the ONU forwarding at all.
Bitmask, DECIMAL. Passed as `omci_app -cb`. Each bit loads one plugin from lib/features; the field below decodes it against this image.

Bitmask, DECIMAL. On the stock firmware it is passed as `omci_app -cme`. On this image omcid reads two bits of it: 0x40 (64) creates the CTC ONU capability entity (class 65529) at MIB reset, as the stock firmware does; 0x100 is `cf_apply_customized_veip_slot_id`, which is what makes OMCI_VEIP_SLOT_ID take effect at all -- set the slot id without this bit and nothing happens. The other bits are not used here.
Bitmask, DECIMAL. Passed as `omci_app -cmc`. Each bit loads one plugin from lib/features; the field below decodes it.
1 starts omci_app with `-m enable_wq`.
column4: 0=0 — off|1=1 — enable_wq

column3: Answers OK to OMCI operations the stack cannot actually satisfy. Some OLTs refuse to finish provisioning without it.
Read by boa, configd, led, mib and xmlconfig — and NOT by omci_app or checkomci. It does not affect provisioning, which was confirmed from the binaries rather than assumed.

The slot the virtual Ethernet interface point is created in, 2 to 254 (not 128); empty keeps slot 6, the stock default. The VEIP, its UNI-G, the TR-069 server, the cardholder and the circuit pack then have the entity ids of that slot (slot 14: 0x0e01 and 0x010e), so the ids the OLT addresses must match. As on the stock firmware it works only while bit 0x100 of OMCI_CUSTOM_ME is set, and the stock default of that key does not have it; OMCI_CUSTOM_ME is read-only on the Stock keys tab, so set it over ssh with flash set. Without that bit the VEIP stays in slot 6. The stock key, read as a single byte (the MSB of the entity id). Applying re-registers the ONU.

Handed to the europa driver at boot by insert_europa.sh, and read by runsdk.sh to choose which stack starts. This key is not only yours: with PON detection on, pondetect rewrites it and reboots after about 24 seconds of light without PON sync, so a value that changed on its own came from there.
column4: 1=1 — GPON|2=2 — EPON

column3: The first four characters of the serial number, and must match it. Read by the stock firmware only: this image takes the prefix from the serial number.
32 hex characters. Read by the stock firmware only: this image ignores it, and changing the UNI MAC address does not need a new one. Keep the original in backups for the stock slot.
1 is the shipped value. Read by the stock firmware only: this image ignores it.
The device login for SSH and telnet. Not this UI's password, which lives in /etc/config/confd.auth.
The device login for SSH and telnet.

The VLAN untagged frames are placed in on the host-side switch port. Upstream issue #475 reports setting this to 0 as the fix for an ONU that registers but forwards nothing; the shipped values are confirmed to forward correctly on their own, so this is recorded as untried rather than recommended.
As above, for the second switch port.
Whether the resolver addresses below are used or taken from the upstream connection.
column4: 0=0 — from upstream|1=1 — use the addresses below

column3: Writes the decoded OMCI conversation with the OLT. 2 is the parsed form, landing in /tmp/omcilog.par — about 95 KB for a full registration. Reading that exchange is the only way to see what the OLT is actually asking for.
column4: 0=0 — off|1=1 — raw|2=2 — parsed

column3: Which message types to log. 4294967295 logs everything.
Leave at 0. /tmp is an unbounded RAM disk on a device with about 1.5 MB free, so the debug level can exhaust memory; parsed message logging is bounded and is what you actually want.
column4: 0=0 — errors only|1=1 — errors|2=2 — warnings|3=3 — info|4=4 — debug (can exhaust memory)

column3: What `pondetect` does with the PON MAC, every two seconds. On: if the SerDes sees light but never achieves sync for about 24 seconds, it concludes the PON type is wrong, rewrites PON_MODE to the other one and hard-reboots -- so a stick that comes back as EPON after a fibre fault did that to itself. Off does not stop pondetect: it still resets the SerDes CDR on every unsynced sample, it just never touches the flash. Detection is skipped entirely while GPON_SN is the factory default RTKG11111111. Read at boot by runsdk.sh, so a change needs a reboot.
column4: 0=0 — off (CDR reset only, never rewrites PON_MODE)|1=1 — on (may rewrite PON_MODE and reboot)

column3: Never writable here. Like the SerDes mode, getting it wrong can take the link down and with it every way into the device.

The address SSH, this UI and the exporter answer on. A change is a trial: the stick moves to it at once, keeps the old address working beside it, and goes back by itself after 90 seconds unless you press Keep on the new address. This page opens the new address by itself as soon as it answers (the browser asks for the password again there, as it keeps it per address). Nothing is stored before the Keep.
Netmask for the management address, applied with it.

A second, fixed address beside the first (br0:2), for reaching the stick when the first is changed to something you cannot route to; turning it off removes it at once, and a page opened on it stops answering.
column4: 0=0 — off (removes it at once)|1=1 — on

column3: Only used when the second address is on; a change is a trial too, like the management IP. 192.168.100.1 is the common choice.

A list of static routes for the management interface, so the stick can be reached from other subnets without NAT. Empty by default: no routes. Up to 8 entries, one per row: a destination (default, or a network like 10.0.0.0/8 with its host bits zero) and a gateway, which must be inside the management subnet (the first address and netmask, or the second while it is on). Stored as DEST via GW entries separated by commas, e.g. default via 192.168.1.254,10.0.0.0/8 via 192.168.1.1. A destination cannot be listed twice. Routes stay on the management side: nothing is routed to or from the fibre. Anything malformed, more than 8 entries, or a gateway outside the management subnets turns the whole key off in the firmware, so it is refused here before it is written. A change is a trial, like the management IP: applied at once, kept only when you press Keep within the time, else it goes back by itself. In a safe-mode boot the stored routes are not applied, and the page stores the key directly, with no trial.

1 lets the manual VLAN below tag the services; any other value means the stick adds no tag at all, whatever the VLAN ID says, and on a line whose OLT accepts only tagged frames the service then stops unless the router tags the service VLAN itself. Applied at once, without re-ranging the ONU.
column4: 0=0 — transparent: no tag, service stops unless the router tags|1=1 — manual: the stick tags (below)

column3: Who tags the service VLAN; with router tags the stick adds no tag, and on a line whose OLT accepts only tagged frames the service stops unless the router tags the VLAN itself. Stick tags: the ONU adds the VLAN ID and priority below to untagged frames upstream and removes the tag downstream. Router tags (transparent): the ONU adds and removes no tag, every VLAN the OLT carries passes to the router, which tags. Only read when VLAN config mode is 1; any other value is router tags. Applied at once, without dropping the fibre link: the ONU stays in O5 either way.
column4: 1=1 — Stick tags|0=0 — Router tags (transparent): service stops unless the router tags

column3: The C-VLAN omcid adds upstream and removes downstream on the services the OLT provisions, your ISP service VLAN; a VLAN the OLT does not carry stops the service at once, while the ONU stays in O5 and looks healthy. Used only when VLAN config mode is 1 AND manual VLAN mode is 1, and only with a priority set too.

802.1p priority bits carried in the tag; keep the value the ISP uses, since an OLT that maps or filters by priority can drop frames with another one. Same gating as the VLAN ID; an empty priority means no manual tag, as on the stock firmware.

Lets 802.1X EAPOL frames (EtherType 0x888e) cross the stick untagged in both directions while everything else keeps the service VLAN tag. For an ISP that authenticates the line with 802.1X on untagged or VLAN 0 frames while the service itself is on a VLAN: the router can then use one untagged WAN interface, with its supplicant on that same interface. Experimental: run on one line that uses EAP so far. Leave VLAN forward operation override empty with it: the key carries the EAPOL frames itself and does not need or set the override. Off by default, because some ISPs expect EAP on the service VLAN. Used only when VLAN config mode is 1 AND manual VLAN mode is 1, with a VLAN ID and a priority set. Applied at once, without re-ranging the ONU. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 1=1 — on: EAPOL passes untagged|0=0 — off: EAPOL gets the service tag too (the default)

column3: Replaces the forward operation (FwdOp) the OLT set on a VLAN filter, for lines whose OLT filter drops frames the service needs: some send their 802.1X EAP frames on VLAN 0 while the filter (FwdOp 0x10) lets only the service VLAN through, and the router never authenticates; 0x00 lets everything through. Entries separated by commas, each the entity ID of a VLAN filter (class 84 in the OMCI MIB browser; decimal like 4354 or hex like 0x1102) and optionally :FwdOp, e.g. 0x1102:0x00,0x110b:0x00; without a FwdOp, 0x02. The same setting and format as the VLAN Forward Operation page of the stock firmware. The MIB browser still shows the value the OLT set. Empty: no override.
What the OLT authenticates; a serial number the OLT does not know keeps the ONU off the line, with no service, until it is set back. Four-character vendor prefix followed by eight hex digits.

An OLT that checks the PLOAM password refuses the ONU with a wrong one, and the service stays down until it is set back. Stored as the hex of an ASCII string, shown decoded under the field. Many OLTs authenticate on the serial number alone and leave this empty; others require it.
The MAC of eth0, its host port and br0.
The logical ONU id a CTC-profile OLT asks for; such an OLT refuses the ONU with a wrong one, and the service stays down until it is set back. Left empty when the OLT does not require one.
The password that goes with the LOID; a wrong one keeps the ONU off a CTC-profile OLT that checks it.
The value omcid actually answers when it differs from LOID. Saving LOID writes this too.
As above, for the password.

What the OLT is told image 0 runs (software image entity, 14 characters at most). An OLT that provisions only the identity it expects can leave the ONU in O5 with management and no service when it reads another value.
What the OLT is told image 1 runs. An OLT that provisions only the identity it expects can leave the ONU in O5 with management and no service when it reads another value.

The equipment id the OLT reads in ONU2-G (20 characters at most). The stock firmware reports IGD. An OLT that provisions only the identity it expects can leave the ONU in O5 with management and no service when it reads another value.

ONU2-G OMCC version, decimal. 128 (0x80) is what this image and the stock firmware report. An OLT that provisions only the identity it expects can leave the ONU in O5 with management and no service when it reads another value.

ONU2-G vendor product code, decimal. 15 is what this image and the stock firmware report. An OLT that provisions only the identity it expects can leave the ONU in O5 with management and no service when it reads another value.

The hardware version the OLT reads in ONU-G (14 printable ASCII characters at most), which some OLTs whitelist. Reported only while the ONU identity switch is on; otherwise the device id. Leave it empty to report the device id: an empty value removes the key. A longer value, or one with a character outside printable ASCII, is ignored whole rather than cut, since a truncated version is a different version. Read by this image, not the stock firmware. An OLT that provisions only the identity it expects can leave the ONU in O5 with management and no service when it reads another value.

What omcid does when the OLT starts a software download to this ONU. Accept answers the download and discards the image; reject refuses it. Either way nothing is installed, flashed or rebooted, and the software image entity only reports the image as activated and committed so the OLT is satisfied. Unset is accept. Read at every download step, so a change is in effect at once. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: accept=accept — answered, then discarded (the service is not touched)|reject=reject — refused (the service is not touched)

column3: 1 answers a Create, Set or Get of a managed entity class omcid has no model for with success, instead of the standard unknown-entity error; off (0 or unset) keeps the error. Turn it on only for an OLT that stalls its provisioning at such an answer, after logread shows event=unknown_me for the class it stops at. The risk: if that entity carried part of a service (a VLAN rule, a queue, a vendor extension), the part is silently missing while the OLT believes it is in place, so the ONU reaches O5 and looks provisioned while the service may not work, and an OLT that audits the MIB against what it wrote can resynchronise over and over. Check the service afterwards. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 0=0 — off (unknown entity, the standard answer)|1=1 — on (answer success; a part of a service may be silently missing)

column3: Whether the stick has a virtual Ethernet interface point (VEIP). Create (the default) is what the stick has always done. None presents the ONU as pure PPTP: no VEIP, no UNI-G of the VEIP, no TR-069 server, and no cardholder or circuit pack of the VEIP slot, five entities fewer in the MIB upload; only for an OLT that provisions the physical UNI and never a bridge port on a VEIP. Applying re-registers the ONU, so the fibre service drops meanwhile. A separate key from the VEIP slot because the stock firmware reads that one as a slot number only. Read by omcid at start and on SIGHUP, by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 1=1 — create the VEIP (the default)|0=0 — none: a PPTP-only ONU (an OLT that bridges to a VEIP stops provisioning)

column3: The three vendor-private entities the ONU creates for itself (350, 370 and 373; 373 carries a third-party product string), as the stock firmware does. Leave them out only for an OLT that rejects or mistrusts them. Applying re-registers the ONU, so the fibre service drops meanwhile. Read by omcid at start and on SIGHUP, by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 1=1 — create them (the default, as stock)|0=0 — leave them out

column3: Lets the OLT reboot the stick over OMCI. Off by default. On, a Reboot of the ONU-G is answered with success and the stick restarts a second later (the fibre is down for the boot); acknowledge only answers success and does not reboot, for an OLT that insists on a successful answer; off, it is refused with command not supported. Read each time the OLT sends a Reboot, so a change is in effect at once. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 0=0 — off (refuse the OLT reboot)|1=1 — on (the OLT can reboot the stick)|2=2 — acknowledge only (answer OK, do not reboot)

column3: Entities of a native ONU that this stick has no model for, answered with bytes you copy from that ONU. Up to 16 entries, one per row: the class (1 to 65535), the instance (0 to 65535, decimal or 0x hex), the attribute (1 to 16) and its bytes in hex (optional 0x, 1 to 25 bytes), e.g. 200:0x8001:1:0x0011aa. Rows with the same class and instance are one entity with several attributes: it is listed in the MIB upload, a Get of it answers the attributes asked for that it has, and a Get of any other instance of the class is answered as unknown. Instance and attribute both set to any (the form CLASS:HEX) answers every instance of the class, and the entity is not in the MIB upload. Only a class omcid has no model of its own for is answered: an implemented class is never overridden. A slot cannot be listed twice, and a class cannot be in both forms. Empty removes the key. Anything malformed turns the whole key off in omcid, so it is refused here before it is written. Applying re-registers the ONU, so the OLT provisions it again and the fibre service drops meanwhile. The bytes stay on this stick, in odi.conf, are not logged and are redacted from the diagnostics bundle. Read by omcid at start and on SIGHUP, by this image, not the stock firmware.

Whether the host port (the SFP edge, toward the router) runs auto-negotiation. On, the default and what the stock firmware does, negotiates 1000BASE-X with the router; off forces 1000BASE-X full duplex, for a router port with auto-negotiation off. Changed only from Config, Network, Host port, as a trial that reverts by itself after two minutes unless kept; never by Save. A boot whose forced link does not come up runs auto-negotiation and says so; three short power cycles in a row clear it. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: on=on — negotiate (the default)|off=off — forced 1000BASE-X full duplex

column3: How the host port (the SFP edge, toward the router) talks to the router. fiber1g, the default and what the stock firmware does, is 1000BASE-X (Fiber 1G, the most compatible); 2500basex is 2500BASE-X, for a router port that runs 2.5G, with auto-negotiation off; hisgmii is HiSGMII. Changed only from Config, Network, Host port, as a trial that reverts by itself after two minutes unless kept; never by Save. A 2500basex boot that sees no link runs Fiber 1G and says so; three short power cycles in a row clear it. While it is not fiber1g, HOST_AUTONEG cannot be tried. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: fiber1g=Fiber 1G — 1000BASE-X (the default)|2500basex=2.5G — 2500BASE-X, auto-negotiation off|hisgmii=HiSGMII

column3: The remote syslog collector, as `host` or `host:port`; empty (the shipped default) leaves remote logging off. Read by this image, not the stock firmware. Letters, digits, dots and hyphens only, optional port 1-65535.

The NTP server, as `host` or `host:port`; empty (the shipped default) leaves the NTP client off. Read by this image, not the stock firmware. Passed to busybox `ntpd -p`, which resolves the string with the shared host2sockaddr/str2sockaddr helper -- a bare host defaults to port 123, and a trailing `:port` overrides it. Letters, digits, dots and hyphens only, optional port 1-65535.

Lets the stick follow the IGMP of the router behind it and apply what the OLT provisions for multicast: one row per group, and the group limit and access lists of the profile. Experimental, and not yet run against a real multicast stream. Off, multicast is flooded as it always was. Saving restarts the snooping daemon; the fibre service is not touched. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 1=1 — on|0=0 — off: multicast is flooded (the default)

column2: Drop unjoined multicast from the fibre (experimental)
column3: Also drops multicast from the fibre that no host asked for, so a group nobody joined stays off the host link. Experimental. It is the one part of snooping that can cut a stream, so it is a separate switch and off by default. Does nothing while IGMP snooping is off. Saving restarts the snooping daemon; the fibre service is not touched. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 1=1 — drop unjoined multicast|0=0 — snoop only, drop nothing (the default)

column3: Snoops IPv6 multicast the way IGMP snooping does for IPv4, on the same multicast profile: one row per group, and the group limit and access lists of the profile. Router advertisements, neighbour discovery and DHCPv6 are never pruned. With the drop of unjoined multicast on, unjoined IPv6 groups are dropped too. Experimental. Off, IPv6 multicast is flooded as it always was. Does nothing while IGMP snooping is off. Saving restarts the snooping daemon; the fibre service is not touched. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 1=1 — on|0=0 — off: IPv6 multicast is flooded (the default)

column2: Stay dark when the OLT disables this ONU (experimental)
column3: Keeps the stick switched off, laser included, once the OLT has disabled it, across restarts and power-offs, until the OLT enables it again, as G.984.3 asks. Experimental. On by default. To get out of a kept disable, set this to 0 and reboot, or run /etc/scripts/gpon-hold.sh clear; with 0 the record of the disable stays, so turning this on again brings the hold back until that clear. A safe-mode boot keeps the PON off and leaves the hold in place. Read at boot, so a change needs a reboot. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 1=1 — stay disabled until the OLT enables it (the default)|0=0 — leave the disabled state on any restart

column3: Makes the stick tell the OLT it is restarting on purpose, just before an orderly restart or power-off, so the OLT can tell that from a lost ONU. Experimental. Off by default, because what the OLT does with it is not known: one that gets it without a restart following may drop and re-activate the ONU. Read at boot, so a change needs a reboot. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 1=1 — send Dying_Gasp before a reboot|0=0 — do not send it (the default)

column2: Laser on an unverified laser driver (danger)
column3: Switches the laser on even when the laser driver chip is not the one this image was validated with. Off, such a stick keeps the laser off and refuses to activate on the fibre. A laser that lights outside its timeslot takes down every other ONU on the OLT port, so set it only on a port with no other ONU. Read at boot, so a change needs a reboot. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 1=1 — laser on, even on an unverified driver|0=0 — laser off on an unverified driver (the default)

column2: Honour an OLT lock of the Ethernet port
column3: Whether the stick obeys the OLT when it locks the Ethernet port. Off by default: the lock is answered and the port stays up, because on this SFP that port is the only way in. On, as on the stock firmware, the host link goes down until the OLT unlocks it, and this page, ssh, syslog and metrics go with it; the stick logs a warning just before. To get back in, unplug the fibre and restart the stick, turn this off, then plug the fibre back in; five short power cycles also work (the safe-mode boot turns this setting off). Read at every lock, so a change is in effect at once. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 0=0 — ignore the lock: the port stays up (the default)|1=1 — honour the lock: the host link goes down

column2: Alloc-ID of a T-CONT the OLT never set
column3: What a T-CONT the OLT has not set reports as its Alloc-ID. Ploam, the default and what the stock firmware does, reports the one the OLT assigned on the fibre; unassigned reports the standard not-assigned value. Use unassigned only with an OLT that sets the Alloc-ID itself and picks the first T-CONT that reports empty; one that reads it back may treat the T-CONT as unusable. Read at every Get, so a change is in effect at once. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: ploam=ploam — the Alloc-ID the OLT assigned by PLOAM (the default)|unassigned=unassigned — report not assigned (0x00FF)

column3: Tells the OLT the stick has 1 or 2 phone ports, so an OLT that offers voice can provision a SIP line on each for the router behind the stick. Experimental. The stick has no phone socket, places no call and registers nothing, and the voice does not reach the router yet: the line can be provisioned and carries nothing. Saving re-registers the ONU, so it interrupts internet while the OLT provisions it again. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 0=0 — no phone port (the default)|1=1 — one phone port|2=2 — two phone ports

column3: The slot of the phone circuit pack, 2 to 254 and not 6, 128 or the VEIP's slot. Empty takes the first free slot from 2 up. Has no effect unless Phone ports is 1 or 2 (this page cannot show that dependency). Saving re-registers the ONU, so it interrupts internet. A value that is not a free slot is ignored by omcid. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.

Lets the router behind the stick tell it whether its SIP client is registered (the Phone tab and the API say how), and shows the OLT that state as the line status instead of "config done". Only a report received in the last 5 minutes counts; without one the line reads "config done", as with the key off. Has no effect unless Phone ports is 1 or 2. Read at every Get, so a change is in effect at once. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 0=0 — off: the line status is "config done" (the default)|1=1 — follow the router's report

column2: Diagnostics for the router (host-side SFP EEPROM)
column3: Whether the router can read the module identity and live diagnostics (temperature, supply voltage, bias current, tx and rx power, alarm and warning flags, and the TX_DISABLE, TX_FAULT and RX_LOS bits) from the stick, as from any SFP with digital diagnostics. On, the default, serves them; off stops serving them. Only on the board revisions that wire the SoC SFP EEPROM emulation to the SFP edge (HSGQ v08 / DFP-34X-2C2 v08); on v06 boards the router reads a separate fixed EEPROM with no diagnostics, whatever this says. Left off in a safe-mode boot. In effect at once, no reboot. Read by this image, not the stock firmware.
column4: 1=1 — serve them (the default)|0=0 — do not serve them
